raw.name: InTe
raw.text: InTe is a group-IIIA metal-monochalcogenide monolayer and a 2D III-VI chalcogenide monolayer, described as a two-dimensional material with inversion symmetry (source: 10.1088/2053-1583/4/1/015017; 10.1016/j.apsusc.2022.153528; 10.1038/s41699-023-00410-3). The pristine monolayer is a nonmagnetic indirect gap two-dimensional (2D) semiconductor, exhibiting a Mexican hat-like energy dispersion at the upper part of the valence band (source: 10.1016/j.mssp.2025.109699). It also exhibits the hidden Rashba effect, which features a unique helical spin texture with two Fermi circles in different bands having the same spin helicity and complete spatial spin separation, where spins with one helicity are located in the top sublayer and spins with the other helicity are in the bottom sublayer, demonstrating an intriguing spin-layer locking phenomenon (source: 10.1038/s41699-023-00410-3).

raw.name: TbTi3Bi4
raw.text: TbTi3Bi4 is a kagome metal that reveals a highly complex landscape of magnetic phases arising from an antiferromagnetic ground state (source: 10.1021/acs.chemmater.4c01449). It exhibits a series of metamagnetic transitions that create at least 5 unique magnetic phase pockets, including a 1/3 and 2/3 magnetization plateau (source: 10.1021/acs.chemmater.4c01449). Additionally, it exhibits sharp switching from positive magnetoresistance (+40%) to negative magnetoresistance (-50%) (source: 10.1021/acs.chemmater.4c01449).

raw.text: Two-dimensional (2D) organometallic frameworks exhibit magnetic anisotropy energy that enhances by 5- to 9-fold (source: 10.1021/acs.nanolett.3c03060). They undergo an antiferromagnetic to ferrimagnetic spin order transformation (source: 10.1021/acs.nanolett.3c03060). They also display bipolar magnetic semiconductor behavior with valence and conduction band edges 100% spin polarized in opposite spin channels, as well as normal semiconductor behavior with zero spin polarization (source: 10.1021/acs.nanolett.3c03060).

raw.label: MaterialSystem
raw.name: Co1/3NbS2
raw.text: Co1/3NbS2 is an intercalated transition metal dichalcogenide with Co atoms in van der Waals gaps, described as an antiferromagnetic van der Waals material and a magnetically intercalated transition-metal dichalcogenide with alternating metallic and highly frustrated magnetic layers (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.105.L121107; 10.1103/wh5t-12fn; 10.1103/PhysRevB.107.235149). It exhibits antiferromagnetic order that is completely suppressed around 1.7 GPa (Tc = ~1.7 GPa suppression pressure, method: elastic neutron scattering; source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.107.235149), electronic conduction anisotropy measured in a wide temperature and pressure range, where transport along and perpendicular to layers respond differently to magnetic ordering and hydrostatic pressure (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.107.235149), and a highly frustrated magnetic subsystem (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.107.235149). The material displays a different orbital character near the Fermi level compared to pristine NbS2 (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.105.L121107), a clear band dispersion in the k(z) direction despite its layered structure (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.105.L121107), and potential for exotic phases such as spin density wave instability via Fermi level tuning (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.105.L121107). Additionally, it exhibits a large transverse Hall conductivity even at zero applied magnetic field and has an intrinsic spin chirality (source: 10.1103/wh5t-12fn).

Janus FeSeX (X = Te) monolayer

raw.text: FeSeTe, studied as a Janus FeSeX (X = Te) monolayer (source: 10.1103/3kkj-s5jk) and as a superconducting sample (source: 10.1021/acsami.4c18021), exhibits multiple properties. When spin-orbit coupling is included, it shows topological states with a finite topological band gap at the Fermi level, accompanied by quantized spin Hall conductivity plateaus and nontrivial topological invariants (spin Chern number = 1, Z2 = 1) (source: 10.1103/3kkj-s5jk). The chemical asymmetry of the Janus structure breaks both out-of-plane mirror and inversion symmetries, leading to d-wave altermagnetism characterized by anisotropic exchange interactions and momentum-dependent spin splittings even in the absence of spin-orbit coupling (source: 10.1103/3kkj-s5jk). Phonon dispersion analyses confirm its dynamical stability (source: 10.1103/3kkj-s5jk). Additionally, strain-dependent calculations demonstrate that the magnitude of the altermagnetic exchange splitting (As) can be efficiently tuned by biaxial strain (source: 10.1103/3kkj-s5jk). Regarding superconductivity, the superconducting transition temperature Tc zero increased marginally for the AFM/FST sample (source: 10.1021/acsami.4c18021).

content.text: recently discovered two-dimensional magnetic systems
systems with chiral spin textures, such as magnetic skyrmions
magnetic systems with two-dimensional geometry

raw.label: MaterialSystem
raw.name: two-dimensional magnetic systems
raw.text: Two-dimensional magnetic systems (mat_10_1103_PhysRevB_98_195439_1) are recently discovered magnetic systems with two-dimensional geometry (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.108.045414; 10.1103/7zfd-p48s) that include systems with chiral spin textures, such as magnetic skyrmions (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.98.195439). These systems exhibit a topological Hall effect, which arises from asymmetric carrier scattering on individual chiral spin textures (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.98.195439). They also exhibit magnon-plasmon hybridization, involving magnon-plasmon coupling and hybridization in ferromagnetic (FM) and anti-ferromagnetic (AFM) systems (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.108.045414). Additionally, they exhibit phase alignment reemergence, where the spin structure in a 2D magnetic system can be made to spontaneously reemerge through phase alignment (source: 10.1103/7zfd-p48s), and spatiotemporal diffraction of magnetic moments, where the evolution of magnetic moments in two-dimensional (2D) magnetic systems can be mapped into a spatiotemporal diffraction process (source: 10.1103/7zfd-p48s).

raw.name: GaN
raw.text: GaN (gallium nitride) is a IIIA-nitride binary compound that exists as a two-dimensional (2D) honeycomb-type graphene-like monolayer (g-GaN) and as bulk material. It is a wide-band-gap semiconductor and cornerstone material for power electronics, with reported band gap values of 1.98 eV (indirect, via first-principle calculations; source: 10.1016/j.physb.2022.414367) and 1.95 eV (indirect; source: 10.1016/j.surfin.2022.101898). The pure GaN monolayer is nonmagnetic (source: 10.1016/j.jpcs.2015.12.002) and exhibits semiconductor behavior (source: 10.1016/j.surfin.2022.101898). It maintains electronic stability under intense electric fields (source: 10.1021/acsnano.5c15014). The static dielectric constant and refractive index of g-GaN monolayer are 1.61 and 1.57, respectively (via first-principle calculations; source: 10.1016/j.physb.2022.414367). Vacancies introduce defect levels in the band gap (source: 10.1016/j.apsusc.2017.10.136). The small adsorption energy of all gas molecules on pristine g-GaN suggests physisorption characteristics; specifically, CO, H₂S, and NO adsorbed on intrinsic g-GaN are physisorption, and CO adsorbed on alkali metals doped g-GaN monolayer is also physisorption (sources: 10.1016/j.apsusc.2020.147275, 10.1016/j.jpcs.2020.109857). p-doping of g-GaN is obtained due to charge transfer from the g-GaN layer to superhalogens (source: 10.1016/j.vacuum.2023.112304). The material exhibits half-metallicity due to its half-filled quasi-flat band (source: 10.1021/acs.jpclett.1c03966). High-efficient spin injection in GaN is achieved at room temperature using van der Waals h-BN films as a tunnel barrier (source: 10.1186/s11671-022-03712-5). GaN is used as a component in AlN/GaN heterostructures (source: 10.1002/adfm.202009771), AlN/GaN hybrid heterojunctions (source: 10.1016/j.commatsci.2020.109860), two-dimensional GaN/SiC heterostructures (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.95.045302), and as a polarizable semiconductor layer in van der Waals heterostructures (source: 10.1021/acsami.0c21532). It is also used as a bulk barrier material in heterostructures (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.111.195301), a semiconductor substrate material (source: 10.1016/j.apsusc.2021.150637), and in heterobilayers (source: 10.3390/nano15110832). The material has been recently synthesized as 2D GaN between graphene and SiC or wurtzite GaN substrate (source: 10.1021/acs.jpclett.1c03966).

ferroelectric layered hybrid organic-inorganic perovskite

raw.label: MaterialSystem
raw.name: (AMP)PbI4
raw.text: (AMP)PbI4 is a two-dimensional Dion-Jacobson perovskite (source: 10.1021/acsnano.5c11545) and a ferroelectric layered hybrid organic-inorganic perovskite (HOIP) (source: 10.1038/s41524-020-00450-z). At room temperature, it exhibits a circular polarization degree of 52% in photoluminescence, as measured by steady-state circularly polarized photoluminescence (source: 10.1021/acsnano.5c11545). The material demonstrates ferroelectricity with polarization tunable by ferroelectric polarization (source: 10.1038/s41524-020-00450-z). It shows an extraordinarily large Rashba anisotropy that is tunable by ferroelectric polarization (source: 10.1038/s41524-020-00450-z), and upon polarization reversal, the major and minor axes of the Rashba anisotropy ellipse in k-space are interchanged—a pseudo rotation (source: 10.1038/s41524-020-00450-z). The spin texture chirality is inverted upon polarization reversal (source: 10.1038/s41524-020-00450-z). The material has a spin relaxation time exceeding 20 ns, as determined by time-resolved circularly polarized photoluminescence (source: 10.1021/acsnano.5c11545). The spin diffusion coefficient and spin diffusion length both closely match those of excitons (source: 10.1021/acsnano.5c11545).

raw.name: CuInP2S6
raw.text: CuInP2S6 is a layered metal thiophosphate and a two-dimensional rare-earth/transition metal halide derivative, classified as a van der Waals ferroelectric material, a 2D van der Waals antiferroelectric material, a ferroelectric insulator, a low-symmetry ferroelectric material, and a monolayer van der Waals multiferroic material in heterostructures. It exhibits ferroelectricity with reversible polarization direction (source: 10.1039/d5nr01155h) and spontaneous geometric symmetry breaking leading to ferroelectric polarization (source: 10.1021/acs.jpclett.1c02782), including polarized states (P up and P down) in ferroelectric monolayers (source: 10.1039/d0tc00143k). The material shows remanent ferroelectric polarization with polarization-enhanced Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction (DMI) lowering domain wall formation energy (source: 10.1002/adma.202500534). It also exhibits room temperature ferrielectric polarization (source: 10.1016/j.mtcomm.2023.105840), high degrees of phonon anharmonicity (source: 10.1016/j.mtcomm.2023.105840), and short phonon lifetimes of less than 1 ps (source: 10.1016/j.mtcomm.2023.105840). Additionally, CuInP2S6 demonstrates anomalous polarization switching and the formation of quadrupole-well ferroelectric states (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.108.L161406), and its ferroelectric layer is originally in the paravalley state (source: 10.1039/d0tc01680b). The material is used as a ferroelectric monolayer (source: 10.1002/adfm.202104452), a ferroelectric van der Waals material as a spacer (source: 10.1038/s41565-025-02065-1), a two-dimensional material to verify the bend-sliding model (source: 10.1103/v635-zwm4), a monolayer ferroelectric material (source: 10.1039/d0tc04272b), a van der Waals ferroelectric material (source: 10.1002/adma.202500534), a ferroelectric component of 2D van der Waals heterostructures (source: 10.1016/j.mtphys.2022.100803), a van der Waals ferroelectric substrate (source: 10.1103/6wmg-hxdq), a ferroelectric van der Waals material (source: 10.1002/adfm.202528029), a ferroelectric monolayer material (source: 10.1016/j.commatsci.2025.113953), a 2D ferroelectric material (source: 10.1039/d0tc01680b), a two-dimensional material used as a base for substitution (source: 10.1016/j.physb.2025.417605), and a layered van der Waals material (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.108.L161406).

raw.name: VO2
raw.text: VO2 is a transition metal dioxide that can exist in the 1H structure (source: 10.1016/j.cocom.2024.e00896) and as a molecule (source: 10.1016/j.physb.2021.413245). It is a non-van der Waals solid (source: 10.1016/j.nantod.2021.101272) from which a monolayer can be exfoliated from bulk VO2 (source: 10.1039/d3tc03178k). VO2 is a phase-change material that exhibits a reversible metal-to-insulator transition between metallic and insulating states (source: 10.1016/j.matt.2020.04.001). It can also be formed as a reaction product at the interface of VSe2 and MoO3 (source: 10.1021/acsami.9b16822).

content.text: two-dimensional material with zigzag edges

raw.label: MaterialSystem
raw.name: zigzag bilayer phosphorene nanoribbon
raw.text: Zigzag bilayer phosphorene nanoribbon (ZBLPNR) is a two-dimensional material with zigzag edges (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.98.205401). Its band-gap modulation is investigated by the ribbon width and perpendicular electric field (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.98.205401). The ZBLPNR exhibits two nearly degenerate quasiflat edge modes at the Fermi level, isolated from the bulk states (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.98.205401). Due to the existence of these quasiflat bands at the Fermi level, in the absence of an electric field, a sharp peak in the RKKY interaction is seen (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.98.205401). The electrically tunable RKKY interaction of ZBLPNRs is expected to have important consequences on the spintronic application of a biased ZBLPNR, and is tunable via perpendicular electric field (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.98.205401). In the presence of a large bias potential, a beating pattern of the RKKY oscillations occurs when two magnetic impurities are located inside the ZBLPNR (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.98.205401). For large distances, the RKKY interaction falls off as R^-5 for moments located on the zigzag edge, whereas for those placed at interstitial sites it decays as R^-3 (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.98.205401).

raw.label: MaterialSystem
raw.name: altermagnet
raw.text: Altermagnets are a recently discovered class of magnetic materials, classified as the third magnet alongside conventional antiferromagnetism and ferromagnetism, characterized by zero net magnetization but spin-polarized bands induced by broken time-reversal symmetry, featuring spin-split band structures without net magnetization (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.111.174436, 10.1103/ssb5-vm9b, 10.1103/PhysRevB.111.104432). They are collinear compensated Néel ordered magnets, collinear symmetric-compensated antiferromagnets with intrinsic spin splitting, or unconventional antiferromagnets with non-relativistic spin-splitting, defined by combined rotational and time-reversal symmetry breakings (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.111.174436, 10.1103/PhysRevB.110.014442, 10.1007/s11433-024-2567-6, 10.1103/PhysRevB.108.144418). These materials exhibit large or strong momentum-dependent spin splitting governed by distinctive magnetic symmetries or enforced by crystal symmetry, with zero net magnetization but non-zero spin splitting (source: 10.1103/mslj-zz6t, 10.1103/vrpg-stnt, 10.1103/PhysRevLett.133.106601). Altermagnets feature antiparallel spin sublattices with d-, g-, or i-wave spin order (X-wave magnets with X = d, g, i), yielding non-relativistic spin splitting without net magnetization, and are characterized by momentum-dependent alternating spin polarization and zero net magnetization (source: 10.1103/zt4l-y18j, 10.1103/7bss-9yxb, 10.1103/sw4z-f5fl). Specific variants include centrosymmetric altermagnets, two-dimensional altermagnets, two-dimensional d-wave altermagnets (including dx2-y2-wave), two-dimensional d-wave metallic altermagnets, and disordered altermagnetic metals used in AM/FI heterostructures (source: 10.1016/j.physb.2025.417475, 10.1103/jy4r-d579, 10.1016/j.physb.2026.418721, 10.1016/j.aop.2025.170273, 10.1103/k3xb-8pts, 10.1038/s41535-025-00827-7, 10.1103/4txy-gy8f, 10.1103/gr5n-174c, 10.1103/mslj-zz6t, 10.1103/PhysRevB.109.125403). They exhibit spin-split band structures, with intrinsic anisotropic spin splitting, and in two-dimensional d-wave altermagnets, topologically protected spin-polarized Dirac points (source: 10.1103/nsky-zmzp, 10.1103/PhysRevB.111.174436, 10.1103/PhysRevB.109.L201404, 10.1103/PhysRevB.111.224406). Properties include angular momentum radiation minimally reactive to Rashba spin-orbit coupling at low altermagnet interaction strength but with drastic oscillations at a critical point; energy radiation highly sensitive to Rashba spin-orbit coupling with a saturation effect beyond a particular value, with peak emission lower than graphene; and optical conductivity affected by RSOC strength, altermagnet interaction strength, and Néel vector direction (source: 10.1103/jy4r-d579). For small wave vectors k, the decay rate scales as k^5 with a direction-dependent prefactor (source: 10.1103/b5vs-ldpm). Electronic and magnonic Hall currents are calculated in gapped phases, where gapped phases with finite Chern, spin Chern, and/or chirality Chern numbers emerge under different symmetry-breaking mass terms (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.111.224406). Numerical calculations of electronic heat capacity (EHC) along high-symmetry directions (r-X and r-Y) reveal pronounced directional asymmetries and direction-dependent helical spin textures (source: 10.1016/j.physb.2026.418721). Altermagnets provide a platform for finite-momentum superconductivity, with several pair-density-wave states emerging in two-dimensional d-wave metallic altermagnets, and nonreciprocal superconductivity (superconducting diode effect) observed in altermagnetic systems (source: 10.1016/j.aop.2025.170273, 10.1103/PhysRevB.110.024503). The intrinsic anisotropic spin splitting can result in a gapless superconducting state exhibiting spin-polarized segmented Fermi surfaces with coexisting spin-singlet and spin-triplet pairings of d-wave character, along with a pair of mirage gaps at finite energy (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.109.L201404). Mixing in an isotropic photoinduced s-wave correction is reported (source: 10.1103/mslj-zz6t). Zero-energy Majorana corner modes (MCMs) result from certain configurations (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.108.205410). Canonical altermagnets are used for comparison (source: 10.1088/0256-307X/42/11/110713).

chemically bonded layered Na2IrO3
Honeycomb Na2IrO3 is a prototype spin-orbit Mott insulator and Kitaev magnet.

raw.label: MaterialSystem
raw.name: Na2IrO3
raw.text: Na2IrO3 is a honeycomb lattice compound with transition metal ions and strong spin-orbit coupling (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.99.064425), described as a chemically bonded layered material (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.110.L020403) and a honeycomb Kitaev material (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.99.205119). It is a prototype spin-orbit Mott insulator (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.108.235130) and a spin-orbit assisted Mott insulator with a honeycomb arrangement of ions (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.101.235415), hosting bond-dependent Kitaev interactions (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.102.155134) and frustrated bond-dependent anisotropic magnetic interactions (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.99.064425). The material exhibits insulating behavior as a Mott insulator (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.108.235130). Magnetically, Na2IrO3 orders below 7 K with a zero-field zigzag phase and zigzag order within the honeycomb planes (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.95.180411), detected in the zigzag ordered phase (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.96.241107) and described as a zero-field zigzag phase (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.101.174444); the spin liquid whose spinon condensation leads to the zigzag magnetic order was observed in Na2IrO3 and alpha-RuCl3 (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.99.205119). It has an antiferromagnetic zigzag ground state on the honeycomb lattice (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.96.064430), and two-dimensional zigzag magnetic correlations in NaxIrO3 are similar to those in Na2IrO3 in terms of ordered magnetic moment direction and three dynamically fluctuating zigzag orders (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.106.075157). The magnetic ordering transition is known for bulk Na₂IrO₃ (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.101.235415). Electronic transport measurements allow deduction of values for the density of states and localization length (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.101.235415).

raw.name: SrTiO3
raw.text: SrTiO3 (STO) is a perovskite oxide material, a band insulator, and a quantum paraelectric that serves as a standard substrate for a wide range of high-temperature superconducting cuprates, colossal magnetoresistive manganites, and multiferroics, and is used as a substrate or component in oxide heterostructures, superlattices, and interfaces (source: 10.1002/adma.201906003, 10.1002/admi.201900547, 10.1103/PhysRevB.106.L201103, 10.1103/PhysRevLett.129.187201, 10.1021/acsaelm.5c01829, 10.1007/s12274-023-5662-6). It is a nonmagnetic perovskite oxide, a wide band-gap insulator, and a transition metal oxide that forms two-dimensional electron gases (2DEGs) at its surfaces and interfaces, exhibiting properties such as superconductivity, high electron mobilities at low temperature, efficient spin-charge interconversion, and Rashba spin-orbit coupling (source: 10.1021/acs.nanolett.5c02127, 10.1103/PhysRevResearch.6.023074, 10.1002/adma.201906003). The 2DEGs at SrTiO3-based homo- and heterostructures provide new opportunities for electronics and spintronics, and the carrier type can be switched from p-type (2DHG) to n-type (2DEG) by controlling the Fe thickness, with X-ray radiation leading to on-demand formation of a 2DEG in STO (source: 10.1002/admi.201900547, 10.1002/adma.201906003, 10.1002/adfm.201900645). A 2DHG with an ultrahigh mobility of 24,000 cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹ is demonstrated using an interface between STO and a thin amorphous FeOy layer (source: 10.1002/adma.201906003). The t2g band structure of SrTiO3-based two-dimensional electron gases plays a role in features such as the superconducting dome, high-mobility transport, and the magnitude of spin-orbit coupling (source: 10.1103/PhysRevMaterials.9.056202). Nonparabolic electronic states in SrTiO3 2DES show an E-k dispersion incorporating both linear and parabolic relations (source: 10.1103/PhysRevResearch.6.043231). Ballistic transport is analyzed in contacts realized at the (001) interface between LaAlO3 and SrTiO3, with conductance quantization observed at low energies (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.103.235120). The Edelstein effect enables interconversion of charge and spin currents through direct and inverse Edelstein effects, with record efficiencies at low temperature but more modest effects at room temperature, and the conversion efficiency is enhanced by nearly one order of magnitude (source: 10.1103/PhysRevResearch.6.023074). Nonlocal spin-transport on two-dimensional surface-conducting SrTiO3 without a ferromagnetic spin-injector is demonstrated via the spin Hall effect and inverse spin Hall effect, with a spin diffusion length λ_s ≈ (1.23 ± 0.7) μm at 2 K, a spin lifetime τ ≈ 49 ps, and a spin Hall angle γ ≈ (0.25 ± 0.05), along with an anisotropic spin-signal consistent with Hanle precession of a pure spin current (source: 10.1021/acs.nanolett.1c01607). X-ray irradiation induces the formation of a metallic state at the SrTiO3/Si interface (source: 10.1002/adfm.201900645). The mobility of ionic species is considerably enhanced as compared to the bulk in SrTiO3-based heterostructures (source: 10.1002/adma.202004132). A 2DEG is formed at the interface of gamma-Al2O3/SrTiO3 (source: 10.1021/acs.jpclett.2c00384). Additional emergent properties include colossal ionic conductivity and giant thermoelectric effect, most of which emerge in a 2DEG formed at an STO interface (source: 10.1002/adma.201906003). SrTiO3 is also used as a substrate for FeSe growth, a component of LaAlO3/SrTiO3 heterostructures, and a substrate material with TiO2-terminated (001) surface, undergoing a structural phase transformation around 105 K (source: 10.1038/NPHYS4186, 10.1103/PhysRevB.96.064401, 10.1002/admi.202201371, 10.1016/j.actamat.2019.09.051).

raw.label: MaterialSystem
raw.name: MXene
raw.text: MXene is a large family of two-dimensional (2D) transition-metal carbides, nitrides, and carbonitrides, often described as a new class of 2D solids, an emerging 2D material, and a rising star of 2D materials, with thickness, composition, and functionalization-dependent outstanding properties. Specific examples include Ti3C2Tx (a 2D titanium carbide in the MXene family, also referred to as 2D Ti3C2Tx MXene sheets, laminated Ti3C2Tx MXene, multilayered Ti3C2Tx MXenes, and 2D Ti3C2Tx MXene film), Ti3CNTx (2D Ti3CNTx MXene), Cr2TiC2Tx (a recently reported magnetic MXene), Mo2TiC2Tx, Mo2CTx (delaminated Mo2CTx MXene), and Zr3C2 and Hf3C2. Ti3C2Tx MXene is one of the most comprehensively studied 2D materials in terms of its adsorptive, transport, and catalytic properties. MXenes exhibit a range of magnetic and electronic properties: small ferromagnetic loops observed below 50 K for Ti3C2TX prepared by hydrofluoric acid (HF) etching of Al layers from Ti3AlC2 (source: 10.1016/j.matchemphys.2022.126155); ferromagnetic hysteresis loops observed for reduced Ti3C2TX (r-Ti3C2TX) up to 150 K, indicating a significant upshift of the paramagnetic to the ferromagnetic transition temperature (source: 10.1016/j.matchemphys.2022.126155); simultaneous ferroelectric and ferromagnetic orders (source: 10.1038/s41699-023-00368-2); negative magnetoresistance present at low temperatures in single flake samples arising from weak localization (source: 10.1021/acsaelm.5c01847) and distinct negative magnetoresistance of -0.4% for Ti3C2Tx (source: 10.1021/acsami.1c18471); Ti3C2 features an extraordinary Curie temperature above 800 K, while those of Zr3C2 and Hf3C2 are above room temperature, as determined by Monte Carlo simulation (source: 10.1039/d1nr00139f); microwave absorption performance with a minimum reflection loss of -41.36 dB at 11.76 GHz at a thickness of 1.94 mm and an effective absorption band of 4.24 GHz in the 13.76-18 GHz range at 1.5 mm thickness (source: 10.1021/acsanm.2c04062); the carrier density justifies Ti₃C₂Tₓ being described as a 2D metal (source: 10.1080/21663831.2017.1333537); a band gap increased to 1.44 eV after doping with La³⁺ ion (source: 10.1016/j.mtchem.2020.100271); density of apparent mobile carriers in Ti₃C₂Tₓ is approximately 1 × 10¹⁴ cm⁻² (10²⁸ cm⁻³) under a single-band model assumption (source: 10.1080/21663831.2017.1333537); significant Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction exists in 2D multiferroic MXenes, with magnitude scaling with electric dipole strength (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.108.054440); for MXenes with surface Ti atoms (e.g., Ti3C2Tx and Ti2CTx), the Ti L-edge spectra are significantly modified compared to their parent MAX phase, while for MXenes without surface Ti atoms (e.g., Mo2TiC2Tx and Cr2TiC2Tx), minimal changes in spectral features are observed (source: 10.1088/2053-1583/ab68e7); frequency-dependent ferroelectricity in 2D Ti3C2Tx MXene film at room temperature via P-E measurement (source: 10.1038/s41699-023-00368-2); lattice parameters of parent un-doped MXene: a = 5.35 Å, c = 19.2 Å by X-ray diffraction (source: 10.1016/j.mtchem.2020.100271); spin-polarized DFT calculations confirmed that Ti3CNTx possesses magnetic moments (source: 10.1021/acsanm.2c04062); clear evidence of a magnetic transition in Cr2TiC2Tx at approximately 30 K (source: 10.1039/d0nh00343c); strong magneto-electric coupling at room temperature confirmed by magnetic field control of electric polarization (source: 10.1038/s41699-023-00368-2); as-prepared Ti3C2Tx exhibits very weak paramagnetism (source: 10.1016/j.carbon.2019.10.016); MXene is a single dielectric-type loss material, contributing to the microwave absorption performance of Ti3CNTx (sources: 10.1021/acsami.0c00935, 10.1016/j.jpcs.2023.111361, 10.1021/acsanm.2c04062). MXenes are also described as 2D ferromagnets, non-centrosymmetric structures, and dielectric multi-layered structures, gaining attention in electromagnetic wave absorption due to outstanding conductivity and unique layered structures (source: 10.1039/d4ta05088f).

raw.name: CrPS3
raw.text: CrPS3 is a van der Waals antiferromagnetic material, with single-layer CrPS3 predicted to be an antiferromagnetic semiconductor (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.94.184428). It is a member of the MPX3 family, which can exhibit three distinct antiferromagnetic phases (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.106.035137), and is related to compounds such as CrPS4, an air-stable, layered A-type antiferromagnet with a Néel temperature of 36 K (source: 10.1021/acsami.5c25896) and an A-type antiferromagnetic ground state formed by out-of-plane ferromagnetic monolayers with interlayer antiferromagnetic coupling along the c axis below T_N = 38 K (source: 10.1002/adma.202001200). The material exhibits antiferromagnetic ordering with a distinct Néel temperature (source: 10.1039/d5nr02538a), and the ab initio calculations predict that most single-layer MPX3 materials are antiferromagnetic semiconductors (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.94.184428). For CrPS4, the A-type antiferromagnetic ordered ground state has a magnetic moment of 2.78 mu(B) per chromium atom (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.108.155133). The material also exhibits a spin-flop transition at approximately 0.7 T for H parallel to c (source: 10.1002/adma.202001200), a first-order spin reorientation transition at T* ≈ 34 K with magnetic moments realigning from being almost parallel with the c axis in the ac plane to the quasi-1D chains of CrS6 octahedra along the b axis upon heating (source: 10.1002/adfm.202106592), and a paramagnetic state at high temperatures (source: 10.1021/acsami.6b16553). The intrinsic Curie temperature of vdW CrPS4 is 40 K, which can be enhanced up to room temperature by the interfacial effect from graphene (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.108.L100406). The material is a van der Waals antiferromagnet chromium thiophosphate (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.107.L180403), a two-dimensional A-type antiferromagnetic semiconductor (source: 10.1103/PhysRevX.14.041065), and an air-stable A-type antiferromagnet (source: 10.1021/acsami.5c25896). It exhibits a collinear antiferromagnetic state at in-plane fields >7 T and a temperature of 25 K (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.110.224434), and a canted antiferromagnetic state between two adjacent layers under an in-plane magnetic field (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.110.214411). The material also shows a Fano resonance when it experiences a phase transition into the antiferromagnetic state below the Néel temperature (38 K) (source: 10.1021/acsnano.9b08336), and dual-band NIR photoluminescence with bifurcation into fluorescence and phosphorescence (source: 10.1021/acsnano.2c05600). The band gap of CrPS3 is reported as 1.34 eV for bulk, 1.37 eV for monolayer, and 1.35 and 1.30 eV for bilayer and trilayer, respectively, as calculated by SCAN meta-GGA DFT (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.108.155133). The material is also described as a van der Waals antiferromagnet early-transition-metal-based compound (source: 10.1103/PhysRevMaterials.7.064008), a candidate material for dual-switchable ferroelectric altermagnets (source: 10.1021/acs.nanolett.5c03483), and a layered metamagnet with high optical and magnon transport anisotropy (source: 10.1002/adfm.202310206).

raw.name: LaAlO3/SrTiO3
raw.text: The LaAlO3/SrTiO3 system is an oxide heterostructure interface (10.1103/PhysRevLett.126.057701) that forms a two-dimensional electron gas (10.1103/PhysRevB.98.155442, 10.1103/PhysRevMaterials.4.071001, 10.1103/PhysRevLett.128.187401), a quasi-two-dimensional electron gas (q2DEG) (10.1021/acsnano.2c08622), a two-dimensional electron system (10.1103/PhysRevB.97.075136), a 2D electron liquid (10.1103/PhysRevB.95.241107), and a two-dimensional d-electron system (10.1103/PhysRevB.110.235108). It is described as a classical oxide interface with relatively weak magnetism (10.1103/PhysRevB.111.235415), a paradigm oxide interface (10.1103/PhysRevMaterials.3.106001), an insulating oxide heterostructure interface (10.1038/NMAT4857), a SrTiO3-based heterointerface supporting quasi-two-dimensional electron systems (10.1021/acs.nanolett.8b01614), and an interface hosting a two-dimensional electron gas where spin and charge currents can be interconverted (10.1021/acs.nanolett.8b04509). The two-dimensional electron liquid at the (001) interface between band insulators LaAlO3 and SrTiO3 undergoes Lifshitz transition as the interface is doped with carriers (10.1103/PhysRevB.94.155103). At a critical carrier density, two additional orbitals populate at the Fermi level, with a concomitant change in the Fermi surface topology (10.1103/PhysRevB.94.155103). At a critical density, both the thermal and dc conductivities rise sharply to higher values while the Seebeck coefficient shows a cusp (10.1103/PhysRevB.94.155103); beyond a sufficiently large field, multiple cusps appear in the Seebeck coefficient revealing multiple Lifshitz transitions (10.1103/PhysRevB.94.155103). The material exhibits superconductivity (10.1103/PhysRevB.110.235108) and coexistence of superconductivity and ferromagnetism at the LAO/STO interface (10.1103/PhysRevMaterials.3.106001), as well as intriguing gate-tunable magnetism (10.1103/PhysRevB.110.235108). It exhibits Rashba spin-orbital coupling (RSOC) (10.1103/PhysRevB.110.235108), with the two-dimensional electron system (2DES) at the interface known to accommodate gate-tunable Rashba spin-orbit coupling (SOC) (10.1103/PhysRevLett.126.057701). The material exhibits Rashba-split bands modulated by an in-plane magnetic field, with alpha(R) varying with Fermi energy and gate voltage (10.1103/PhysRevMaterials.4.071001). It features a two-dimensional electron gas with anisotropic k-cubic Rashba interaction (10.1103/PhysRevB.98.155442). Spin-orbit coupling causes a threefold spin winding at the Fermi surface (10.1103/PhysRevB.97.075136). An exceptionally strong spin Hall coefficient gamma ~ 0.15 +/- 0.05 is reported (10.1021/acs.nanolett.6b03050). Both D'yakonov-Perel' and Elliott-Yafet mechanisms involve in the spin relaxation at low temperature (10.1021/acs.nanolett.6b03050). The bilinear magnetoresistance response is observed in the 2D electron gas at the interface, with angle-dependent response used to extract alpha(R) (10.1103/PhysRevMaterials.4.071001). Standard analysis hints at hole as well as electron conductance (10.1103/PhysRevB.97.075136). The observed residual magnetoresistance is not related to Coulomb interaction but to weak antilocalization (10.1103/PhysRevB.97.075136). A somehow anomalous beating pattern in low magnetic field regime is found in both the density profile and magnetoresistivity (10.1103/PhysRevB.98.155442). Pronounced zero-bias conductance peaks (ZBCPs) are observed in hybrid junctions composed of the oxide heterostructure LaAlO3/SrTiO3 and an elemental superconductor Nb, showing a domelike dependence on the gate voltage (10.1103/PhysRevLett.126.057701). An interfacial Kondo effect arises from the exchange coupling between the localized d xy state induced by defects and itinerant t 2 g orbitals (10.1103/PhysRevB.110.235108).

raw.name: Zr2S
raw.text: Zr2S is a binary metal-rich chalcogenide monolayer in an anti-MoS2 configuration, also described as a layered bulk electride with anionic excess electrons in the interstitial spaces between cationic layers (source: 10.1103/PhysRevMaterials.7.024409; 10.1016/j.apsusc.2022.152821; 10.1007/s40843-024-2861-2). As a monolayer, it exhibits large perpendicular magnetic anisotropic energy up to 2000 μeV/cell for Hf2X, with the anisotropy energy decreasing by one order of magnitude when the metal atom M changes from Hf to Ti (source: 10.1016/j.apsusc.2022.152821). The system is an intrinsic two-dimensional antiferromagnetic semiconductor, with a magnetic ground state of ferromagnetic ordering in a M atomic layer and antiferromagnetic coupling between two M atomic layers (source: 10.1016/j.apsusc.2022.152821). Additionally, it displays massive Dirac nodal-line states arising from Zr-4d cationic and interlayer anionic electrons (source: 10.1103/PhysRevMaterials.7.024409). In its layered bulk form, Zr2S is nonmagnetic (source: 10.1103/PhysRevMaterials.7.024409).

raw.name: Hf2S
raw.text: Hf2S is a binary metal-rich chalcogenide monolayer and a specific member of the MSene family, described as a nonmagnetic layered electride in its pristine form (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.105.L220401) and as a monolayer electride Hf₂S (source: 10.1016/j.apsusc.2025.163020) with an anti-MoS2 configuration monolayer (source: 10.1007/s40843-024-2861-2). The pristine system is an antiferromagnetic metal (source: 10.1016/j.apsusc.2025.163020), while other reports describe it as an intrinsic two-dimensional antiferromagnetic semiconductor with a magnetic ground state of ferromagnetic ordering in a M atomic layer and antiferromagnetic coupling between two M atomic layers (source: 10.1016/j.apsusc.2022.152821). In polar stacking bilayer Hf2S, large electric polarization, metallicity, and magnetism coexist in one single-phase material (source: 10.1038/s41524-024-01237-2), with an unexpectedly large out-of-plane electric polarization that survives despite its metallicity and is at least two times larger than that of bilayer BN (source: 10.1038/s41524-024-01237-2). Strong magnetoelectric coupling in this polar stacking bilayer allows the reversal of net magnetic moments with the reversal of electric dipoles (source: 10.1038/s41524-024-01237-2). The monolayers have large perpendicular magnetic anisotropic energy, up to 2000 μeV/cell for Hf2X, and the anisotropy energy decreases by one order of magnitude when the metal atom M changes from Hf to Ti (source: 10.1016/j.apsusc.2022.152821). As a metal Hf2S (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.111.104405), it exhibits layer Nernst and layer thermal Hall effects, which are present in various 2D A-type layered antiferromagnets, producing nonzero transverse charge currents and nonzero transverse heat currents, respectively, in response to a longitudinal temperature gradient field (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.111.104405). Monolayer Hf2S is also used as a prototype (source: 10.1103/rn1l-d6cq).

raw.name: Kitaev magnets
raw.text: Kitaev magnets are spin-orbit coupled Mott insulators with Ising-like magnetic anisotropies (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.106.245107), governed by Ising-like Kitaev coupling K and symmetric off-diagonal Gamma coupling (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.110.214406), and are promising materials for hosting quantum spin liquids and investigating the interplay of topological and symmetry-breaking phases (source: 10.1103/PhysRevResearch.3.023016), providing a realistic description of candidate Kitaev materials within the edge-sharing octahedra paradigm (source: 10.1103/PhysRevResearch.4.043024). These honeycomb lattice Kitaev model materials (source: 10.1209/0295-5075/126/27002; 10.1103/PhysRevB.103.214416) exhibit a range of properties: phonon dynamics influenced by fractionalized spin excitations, with distinct effects from itinerant Majorana fermions and static Z(2) fluxes (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.103.214416); antiferromagnetic zigzag phases (source: 10.1103/PhysRevResearch.4.043024); a large asymmetry in the extent of an intermediate phase for field directions theta = +/- 60° (source: 10.1103/PhysRevResearch.4.043024); Floquet topological magnons and chiral magnon edge modes (source: 10.1209/0295-5075/126/27002); a topologically ordered chiral spin liquid state (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.106.245107); complex multi-sublattice magnetic orders in a wide region of the phase diagram (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.110.214406); pure ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic Kitaev models (source: 10.1103/PhysRevResearch.4.043024); an intermediate phase region with suppressed energy gaps and substantial spin fractionalization (source: 10.1103/PhysRevResearch.4.043024); Ising magnetic order in two-dimensional (2D) Ising spin systems (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.106.245107); a Kitaev spin liquid phase (source: 10.1103/PhysRevResearch.4.043024); an unusual Kitaev(-P) spin liquid phase (source: 10.1103/PhysRevResearch.4.043024); two modulated S-3 x Z(3) magnets (source: 10.1103/PhysRevResearch.3.023016); two exotic S3 magnets (source: 10.1103/PhysRevResearch.3.023016); scalar-chirality order quantified by a coarse-grained scalar-chirality order featuring a counter-rotating modulation on the two spin sublattices (source: 10.1103/PhysRevB.110.214406); and many topological phases with different (or zero) Chern numbers (source: 10.1103/PhysRevResearch.4.043024).

content.text: ordering in a system with full SU(4) symmetry leads to a cascade of discontinuous transitions
The well-known SU(4) symmetry of quantum Hall ferromagnetism for single-layer graphene is recovered as one subgroup of SO(8)
Various phases including the spin nematic phase and the vector chiral phase emerge from an SU(4) symmetric point in the model by the addition of appropriate perturbative interactions.
